## Meta Ads Library Search: How to Find Any Competitor's Ads in 2026


To run a Meta Ads Library search, open facebook.com/ads/library, choose a country, type the competitor's name, select their Page from the dropdown, and filter by active status, platform, media type, and start date. That takes about two minutes, and it shows you every ad they're currently running on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and Audience Network. This guide covers each step, what the Facebook ad library will never tell you, and how to turn competitor ads into your next round of creative. Updated November 2026.

## What the Meta Ads Library shows and what it hides


Meta's Ad Library is a transparency tool, not a spy tool, and the gap between those two things explains most frustration with it. It's free, official, and accurate for what it covers. It was never built to tell you whether an ad is working.


As of November 2026, Meta keeps ads about social issues, elections, and politics in the library for seven years and publishes spend ranges and audience demographics for them. Ads delivered in the EU stay visible for one year with reach and targeting details, a requirement that came with the Digital Services Act. Ordinary commercial ads outside the EU get none of that treatment. They show up while they run and mostly vanish when they stop.


Here's the split for a typical commercial advertiser:


What the library shows What the library hides


Ad creative (image, video, carousel) Ad spend and daily budgets


Primary text, headline, and CTA button Audience targeting and exclusions


Start date and active status Impressions, clicks, and conversions


Platforms the ad runs on ROAS, CPA, or any performance metric


Library ID for each ad Bid strategy and campaign objective


Number of ads sharing the same creative Which ad set or campaign an ad belongs to


Landing page destination (via the CTA) Creative that ran and was switched off (outside the EU and political ads)


Page name, and who's behind it Test structure, audiences, or placements


Don't skip the right-hand column. People see a polished ad in the library and assume it's a winner. The library can't confirm that. It confirms the ad exists and when it started.


## Step-by-step: how to search the Meta Ads Library


You don't need a Facebook account to search, though being logged in makes the interface more stable. Follow these steps in order.


1. **Open the library.** Go to facebook.com/ads/library. Meta also calls it the Meta Ad Library, and the two names point to the same page.
2. **Pick a country.** The library only returns ads that ran in the country you select, so a UK competitor searched under "United States" can look empty. Choose "All" if you aren't sure where they advertise.
3. **Select "All ads."** The other option, issue, electoral, or political ads, is for a different purpose. Commercial competitors live under All ads.
4. **Search by advertiser, not keyword.** Type the brand name and wait for the dropdown. Click the matching Page. This returns that Page's ads only. A keyword search instead scans ad text across every advertiser, which is useful for category research but noisy for one competitor.
5. **Check you have the right Page.** Large brands run multiple Pages for regions, products, and sub-brands. Search each variation, and note the Page ID in the URL so you can return later.
6. **Apply filters.** Set active status, platform, media type, and a date range (covered in the next section).
7. **Open ad details.** Click "See ad details" on any ad to see the Library ID, platforms, and every version of that creative. Click the CTA to see the landing page.
8. **Save what matters.** The library has no good export, so take screenshots, record Library IDs, and note start dates. Without that, you'll redo the search next month.


Keyword search deserves more credit than it gets. Searching a phrase like "free shipping" or a competitor's product name surfaces advertisers you hadn't listed as competitors, and that's usually where the surprises are.


## Filters worth using (and the ones that mislead)


The filters sit on the results page. Four of them change what you learn.


**Active status.** "Active" shows what's running now, which is the cleanest view of a competitor's current thinking. "Inactive" can surface ended ads, but outside the EU and political categories, coverage is thin. Treat an empty inactive view as missing data, not proof the advertiser never ran anything.


**Country.** Re-run the search for each market you care about. A brand might run a discount-led offer in the US and a brand-led message in Germany. You'll miss that if you only check one country.


**Media type.** Filtering to video isolates the formats that usually take the most production budget. If a competitor is running 14 videos and two static images, they've committed to video. If it's the reverse, they're testing cheap.


**Date range.** This filters by start date. It's the best tool for tracking what's new. Set it to the last 30 days, then revisit monthly, and you've got a lightweight monitoring routine.


One trap: the "multiple versions" label. When an ad says it has, for example, 12 versions, the advertiser is running variations of the same creative. That tells you they're testing that concept, which tells you more than the ad itself does.


## Turn competitor ads into creative strategy


Searching is the easy part. The value comes from what you do in the hour after.


### Read longevity as a rough signal


An ad that's been active for 90 days is probably paying for itself, because few advertisers keep funding ads that lose money for three months. It's a heuristic, not proof. Brands with large budgets can tolerate underperformers longer, and some ads run on autopilot because nobody checked. Still, a 90-day-old ad deserves more attention than one that started yesterday.


### Sort by angle, not by brand


Build a simple sheet with one row per ad and tag each with the hook (problem, outcome, proof, curiosity), the offer (discount, trial, guarantee, none), the format, and the landing page type. After 30 or 40 ads, patterns appear. You might find that three of your five competitors lead with a founder story on video while none use customer quotes. That gap is a test worth running.


### Check the landing pages


Ads are half the story. Click through and look at whether the page matches the promise, how long the form is, and what the offer actually costs. Plenty of competitors with strong creative lose people on the page. That's your opening.


### Turn findings into a short test plan


Pick three things: one angle competitors share (so you're not missing table stakes), one angle nobody's using, and one format you haven't tried. Write briefs for each and run them against your current best ad. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is the Facebook Ad Library the same as the Meta Ads Library?


Yes. Meta renamed its products but the tool at facebook.com/ads/library is the same one people call the Facebook ad library, Meta Ad Library, or Meta Ads Library. It covers ads across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and Audience Network.


### Can I see how much a competitor spends on ads?


Not for commercial ads. The library doesn't show spend, budgets, impressions, or performance. Only political and social issue ads include spend ranges. Any tool that gives you a competitor's exact budget is estimating.


### Can I find competitor ads that have already stopped running?


Sometimes. Outside the EU, inactive commercial ads generally drop out of the library. Ads delivered in the EU remain for a year, and political ads for seven years. If you want a record of older creative, capture ads while they're live.


### How do I know if a competitor's ad is working?


You can't know for certain from the library. Longevity is the best proxy: an ad that's run for 60 to 90 days is more likely to be profitable than one that launched last week. Multiple versions of the same creative also signal that the advertiser is scaling a concept.


### Do I need a Facebook account to search the library?


No. The library is public and works without logging in. You'll get the same results either way, though the interface can load more reliably when you're signed in.
